books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Maria W. Stewart, address at Franklin Hall, Boston, September 21, 1832

stimulus.text:
The church: In 1816, Richard Allen and other Black Methodist ministers in Philadelphia formed the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first independent Black denomination in the United States. Allen, who had bought his own freedom from slavery, became its first bishop. Black Methodists had left white-led churches after Black worshippers were pulled from their knees at prayer.

The speaker: "Tell us no more of southern slavery; for with few exceptions, although I may be very erroneous in my opinion, yet I consider our condition but little better than that." — Maria W. Stewart, speaking at Franklin Hall, Boston, September 21, 1832.

The school: In 1833, Prudence Crandall, a white Quaker teacher, opened a school for Black girls in Canterbury, Connecticut. Townspeople attacked the school and forced it to close in 1834.

The stories and songs: Enslaved people told Br’er Rabbit stories, in which the weak rabbit outwits the strong, and made music on fiddles and banjos built from gourds and horsehair, mixing African and Southern traditions.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 B, with the Stewart quotation verbatim from her September 21, 1832 address at Franklin Hall, Boston, and the Crandall facts checked against the Oxford African American Studies Center chronology.

source: original; Stewart quotation is verbatim public-domain text (1832)
stem: Stewart’s main point in the passage is that

options.text: free Black Northerners still lived under oppression as harsh as slavery
Southern slavery was milder than the prejudice Black Northerners faced
options.misconception: She says the Northern condition is little better, not that Southern slavery is mild.

options.text: Black women should leave public speaking to men
options.misconception: Stewart herself is speaking publicly to a mixed audience.

options.text: the North had already given Black Americans full equality
options.misconception: The passage complains of the opposite.

rationales.A: Stewart says: tell us no more of Southern slavery, for our condition is little better. Free life in the North still meant oppression.
rationales.B: Stewart never calls Southern slavery mild. She says the free North is little better, which still leaves slavery terrible.
rationales.C: Stewart is herself a woman speaking in public. Her point is that Black women must speak, not stay silent.
rationales.D: Stewart complains that free Black people lack equality in the North. She does not say they already have it.
rationales.general:
1. Hear Stewart’s comparison. She says: tell us no more of Southern slavery, our condition is little better.
2. Ask who “our” is. Free Black people in the North, listening in Boston.
3. Name the point. Freedom in the North did not mean equality.
Background: Stewart lectured in Boston in 1832, one of the first American women to speak publicly to a mixed audience.
Remember: “little better than” is a comparison, so find both sides of it.
